title: ECI, CAG, Finance Commission, UPSC

cards.b:
A democracy needs referees that the government of the day cannot easily control. The Constitution creates several: the Election Commission of India (Article 324), the Comptroller and Auditor General (Articles 148-151), the Finance Commission (Article 280) and the Union Public Service Commission (Articles 315-323).

Each guards something different: free elections, honest spending, fair sharing of money between Union and states, and merit in public jobs.

UPSC asks about their independence, their effectiveness and recent controversies: the 2023 law on appointing election commissioners, the Special Intensive Revision of rolls, CAG reports on big scams, and the 16th Finance Commission.

For each body, learn four things: its Article, how members are appointed and removed, what it does, and the main criticism.

• Article 324 vests the "superintendence, direction and control" of elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President and Vice-President in the Commission.
  • It was a single-member body until 1989; briefly three members in 1989-90; permanently multi-member since 1993. Today: a Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners, deciding by majority.
  • Removal: the CEC only like a Supreme Court judge (Article 324(5)); other Commissioners only on the CEC's recommendation.
  • Appointment: in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2 March 2023) the Supreme Court said that, until Parliament made a law, a panel of the PM, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice should choose. Parliament then passed the CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023: a selection committee of the PM, the Leader of the Opposition and a Union Cabinet minister named by the PM. Critics say this gives the government a 2-1 majority.
  • Gyanesh Kumar became CEC in February 2025, the first under the new law.

• Prepares electoral rolls, conducts polls, recognises parties and allots symbols (Symbols Order, 1968), and enforces the Model Code of Conduct (a consensus code, not a law).
  • T.N. Seshan (CEC 1990-96) made the Code real and pushed voter ID cards.
  • EVMs used across the country since 2004; VVPAT added from 2013. In April 2024 the Supreme Court refused to order 100% VVPAT matching.
  • Symbol disputes: it gave the Shiv Sena name to the Eknath Shinde faction (February 2023) and the NCP name to the Ajit Pawar faction (February 2024).
  • Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of rolls began in Bihar in 2025 and spread to other states. The Supreme Court upheld the Commission's power to conduct it in May 2026, citing Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act, 1950.

Criticism: slow action on hate speech by leaders, the timing of poll schedules, and questions over the SIR's effect on poor and migrant voters. Praise: it runs the world's largest elections, with nearly 98 crore registered voters in 2024.

Ambedkar called the CAG probably the most important officer under the Constitution, since he guards the public purse.

  • Article 148: appointed by the President; removed only like a Supreme Court judge. Term six years or age 65. Not eligible for further government office.
  • Article 149 and the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971: audits the Union, states and bodies they fund.
  • Article 151: reports go to the President or Governor, who place them before the legislature. The Public Accounts Committee examines them.
  • Kinds of audit: compliance, financial and performance audit (value for money).

Famous reports: 2G spectrum (2010, a "presumptive loss" of ₹1.76 lakh crore) and coal block allocation (2012). They shaped politics before the 2014 election, but critics said the loss figures were speculative.

K. Sanjay Murthy took office as CAG on 21 November 2024.

Weaknesses: appointment by the executive alone, delays in tabling reports, and fewer audit reports in recent years, as critics note.

• Article 280: set up by the President every five years. A chairman with public-affairs experience and four members (Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951).
  • Duties: recommend the share of Union taxes for states (vertical devolution) and how it is divided among states (horizontal), grants-in-aid under Article 275, and measures to augment local bodies' funds.
  • Recommendations are advisory, but the Union has generally accepted the devolution share.

Recent commissions

14th (Y.V. Reddy): raised the share to 42% (2015-20). 15th (N.K. Singh): 41% for 2021-26, as J&K became a Union Territory; it added demographic performance as a criterion. 16th (Arvind Panagariya): report tabled on 1 February 2026; kept 41% for 2026-31, which the government accepted, though many states had asked for 50%.

Debates: southern states say criteria reward population and penalise good performance; states object to cesses and surcharges outside the pool; the Planning Commission's end in 2015 increased the Finance Commission's weight.

• Articles 315-323. Chair and members appointed by the President; six-year term or age 65. Half the members should have at least ten years in government service.
  • Removal (Article 317): by the President for misbehaviour after a Supreme Court inquiry, or for insolvency, outside employment or infirmity.
  • Functions (Article 320): conducts exams for Union services; advises on recruitment rules, promotions and disciplinary matters. Advice is not binding, but departures are reported to Parliament (Article 323).
  • State Public Service Commissions mirror this.

Debates: the long, costly exam and its urban bias; the shift to Paper II CSAT as qualifying (2015); lateral entry (advertised in 2024, then cancelled after objections over reservation); verification scandals (the 2024 case of a probationer's fake disability and caste claims led UPSC to cancel her candidature); and leaks in state commissions and other exams.

The Kothari Committee (1976) and the Baswan Committee (2016) reviewed the exam.

• Separation and checks: Montesquieu's idea that power must check power. Modern writers add "fourth branch" institutions: electoral bodies, auditors and ombudsmen.
  • Guillermo O'Donnell (1998) called this horizontal accountability: state agencies checking other state agencies, in addition to vertical accountability through elections.
  • Pratap Bhanu Mehta and Devesh Kapur, editors of Public Institutions in India (2005), showed how these bodies' performance depends on leadership and norms, not just law.

In India, the Supreme Court has repeatedly linked independence of such bodies to the basic structure. In Anoop Baranwal it said an Election Commission that is not independent can damage democracy itself.

Weak spots:

  • Appointments rest with the executive. Only the ECI got a committee, and even that has a government majority.
  • Post-retirement jobs (as governors, MPs, ministers) can tempt officers.
  • No fixed budgets: most depend on the ministry for staff and money.
  • Delay in action and in tabling reports.

Strengths:

  • Constitutional protection against removal.
  • Strong individuals (Seshan; CAG reports of 2010-12) show what is possible.
  • Courts back them when attacked.

Reforms suggested: collegium-type selection with the Chief Justice (the Dinesh Goswami Committee, 1990, and the Law Commission's 255th Report, 2015, on the ECI); a ban on post-retirement posts; a charged budget from the Consolidated Fund for the ECI; time limits for tabling CAG reports.

• 2023 Act on ECI appointments: challenges pending in the Supreme Court; Gyanesh Kumar appointed CEC (February 2025).
  • SIR of electoral rolls: Bihar (2025), more states in 2025-26; upheld in May 2026.
  • 16th Finance Commission: 41% share for 2026-31; tabled 1 February 2026.
  • GST Council: not one of these four, but another federal body whose recommendations, per Mohit Minerals (2022), are persuasive, not binding.
  • CAG: K. Sanjay Murthy (from November 2024).
  • One Nation, One Election: the 129th Amendment Bill would give the ECI the task of synchronised polls; it is with a JPC.

"Examine the role of the Election Commission in ensuring free and fair elections. Is its independence under threat?"
"The CAG is the guardian of the public purse. Discuss."
"Evaluate the role of the Finance Commission in fiscal federalism."
"Assess the working of the UPSC."

Structure: Article and composition; appointment and removal; functions; landmark episodes (Seshan, 2G, 15th and 16th FC); theory of horizontal accountability; critique and reforms; recent issues (2023 Act, SIR).
